solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Working out FA Chair's in foreign country

indicators.note: something working is in operation and active, so these letters are put to work and rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter by letter, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: The head of the Football Association is busy exercising while abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working out' reads as a gym session, but only 'Working' is the signal; 'out' belongs with the letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The nation at the southern tip of Africa is a country foreign to the British setter and solver.

clue.text: Discussion group remains confused

indicators.note: something confused is muddled up, so the letters lose their original order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A discussion group still has not grasped the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains confused' reads as a verb phrase about the group, but 'remains' is just a word whose letters get shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A seminar is a small class where students meet to talk through a topic with a tutor.

clue.text: Endless call to block French article is excessive

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
a blockage sits inside a passage, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: DUN is a call or demand for payment of a debt, losing its last letter
une is the French feminine word for 'a'

explanation.surface: Constant phone calls stopping a French newspaper piece from running are going too far.
explanation.walkthrough: A dun is an old word for a creditor's demand to pay up, which is why 'call' works here.
explanation.definitionFit: Undue means more than is warranted or appropriate, which is the same as unreasonably large or excessive.

clue.text: Spots on EastEnders area of East London

indicators.note: as spoken by East Londoners, who famously drop the H at the start of words

blocks.note: acne is an outbreak of skin spots

explanation.surface: Pimples on actors from the BBC soap EastEnders, set in a fictional East London borough.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a long-running BBC soap set in East London. A Cockney drops the opening H, so the district is said 'Ackney', which sounds like acne.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackney is a borough in the inner east of London, north of the Thames, well known for its Cockney heritage.

clue.text: Searches around taking a very long time

blocks.note: first meaning: hunts about, as for food
second meaning: a common two-word phrase for lasting an age, run together into one word

explanation.surface: Someone takes forever rummaging about for something.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning only works if you split the answer as FOR AGES, the everyday phrase for something that lasts a very long time.
explanation.definitionFit: To forage is to rummage widely looking for food or supplies, so the verb matches hunting about in every direction.

clue.text: Cyril, late as ever, somewhat embarrassed

indicators.note: somewhat means to a partial degree, so only a part of the run of letters is used

blocks.note: the letters run through the names and words, ignoring spaces and the comma

explanation.surface: Cyril, who is always late, feels a bit sheepish about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer begins inside 'Cyril' and ends inside 'ever'; the commas are surface punctuation only.
explanation.definitionFit: Being uncomfortable and awkward in a social situation is what it means to feel embarrassed or self-conscious.

clue.text: Living with a friend outside Winnipeg, essentially

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letters are kept
being outside something means wrapping around it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: A as written plus MATE, a friend
the two central letters of the eight-letter city

explanation.surface: Someone is living with a pal somewhere on the edge of Winnipeg in Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: Winnipeg has eight letters, so its middle is the fourth and fifth pair; those slot between A and MATE.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, animate describes something alive, possessing life, as opposed to inert or inanimate objects.

clue.text: Hill maybe flipping exhausted idealistic migrant

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards
exhausted means emptied out, so the inner letters go and only the outer ones stay

blocks.note: Damon Hill was a Formula One world champion; 'maybe' shows Hill is one example of the name
first and last letters only

explanation.surface: A tired dreamer on the move, perhaps a man called Hill, is having a terrible time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hill maybe' points to a person called Hill; Damon Hill, the 1996 F1 champion, is the one. 'Flipping' also reads as a mild British swear word in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomadic people roam from place to place rather than settling, just as migrant peoples or birds travel seasonally.

clue.text: Worth lender being bust? It's hell

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so these letters are smashed and reassembled

blocks.note: both words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A bank going bankrupt is pure hell, someone complains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like financial collapse to suit the lender, but it signals breaking up the eleven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The netherworld is the underworld of the dead, the realm below in myth and religion, matching the infernal place.

clue.text: Drove vehicle in competition, joined by winner finally

indicators.note: finally points at the end, so only the closing letter is kept
by means next to, so one piece is placed alongside the other

blocks.note: final letter only
allied means united or joined together

explanation.surface: A driver raced in a motorsport event and was eventually joined by the champion.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the long opening phrase; the wordplay is just the final three words, with the end of 'winner' put in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A rally is a motor race over public or rough roads, so to have rallied is to have driven a car in such an event.

clue.text: Recklessness of some French surgical procedure initially dismissed

indicators.note: dismissing what comes first means the opening letter is removed

blocks.note: des is French for 'some'
an OPERATION, losing its first letter

explanation.surface: A French surgeon rashly sent a patient home before an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: Des is the French partitive article meaning 'some' (as in des pommes, some apples).
explanation.definitionFit: Desperation drives people to act rashly, with no regard for danger, so it can stand for headlong recklessness.

clue.text: Keen to offload home, perfect for one

indicators.note: offloading means getting rid of cargo, so some letters are taken away

blocks.note: intense means keen or ardent
being in is being at home

explanation.surface: Someone eager to sell their house, which would be ideal for a single person.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove IN from the front of INTENSE. 'Perfect' looks like praise of the home but is the grammatical term.
explanation.definitionFit: The perfect is a verb tense, as in 'I have eaten', so it is one example of the category the answer names.

clue.text: Told man makes harsh sounds to expose birds

indicators.note: something told is said aloud rather than written, so the spoken form counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: a knight is a man, a piece in chess
jars are grating, jarring noises

explanation.surface: Someone is informed that a man is making a racket to flush birds out of cover.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords 'man' often means a chess piece; the knight is the one that sounds like a time of day.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightjars are nocturnal insect-eating birds known for their churring calls, so they are an example of birds.

clue.text: Advanced guards extremely tough and physical

indicators.note: the extremes of something are its two ends, so only the first and last letters count
guards stand around what they protect, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: early means ahead of time, advanced
first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Elite security guards are hardened and strong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advanced guards' looks like a military vanguard, but 'Advanced' means ahead of time and 'guards' is the wrapping instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthly describes the material world as opposed to the spiritual, so it means bodily or physical rather than heavenly.

clue.text: Spooner's empty rooms creating problems for Tom?

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the starts trade places

blocks.note: empty means bare; it takes the H sound from the other word
halls are large rooms; it takes the B sound from the other word

explanation.surface: Someone notices that empty rooms are causing trouble for a man named Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom here is a tomcat, a male cat, not a person; the question mark flags that it is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Cats swallow fur while grooming and cough up the clumps, a familiar nuisance for any male cat or tom.

clue.text: Cat emerges from Portuguese maisonette, heading west

indicators.note: something emerging from a place was inside it, so the letters are found within the words
west is leftwards in an across clue, so the letters read from right to left

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A cat comes out of a flat in Portugal and wanders off westward.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across the end of 'Portuguese' and the start of 'maisonette', and must then be read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Siamese is a pale, blue-eyed breed with dark points, originally from Thailand, so it is one kind of domestic feline.

clue.text: Where to enter chatroom with bestie abroad?

indicators.note: abroad can mean widely scattered, so the letters are spread out and rearranged

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for with
taken as written

explanation.surface: How do you get online to talk with your best friend who lives overseas?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' seems to place the best friend overseas, but it signals the shuffle. A bestie is slang for a best friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A chatroom is accessed through a page on the internet, so the answer names the place you go to join one.

clue.text: Escape trouble during fight

indicators.note: during means in the course of, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a bout is a boxing contest
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: A fighter looks for a way out of difficulty mid-bout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' is a verb here, as in 'what ails you?'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bail out is to jump from an aircraft or abandon a situation, which is a way of making an escape.

clue.text: Title of posh male from Elm Road, surprisingly

indicators.note: a surprising result is unexpected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

blocks.note: both words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: An aristocrat unexpectedly lives on an ordinary suburban street called Elm Road.
explanation.walkthrough: The suburban street name makes the noble title seem out of place, which is the surface joke.
explanation.definitionFit: An earldom is the rank or dignity held by an earl, a British nobleman, so it is that aristocrat's title.

clue.text: Scented plant releases aroma, ultimately enthralling one

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the closing letter is kept
to enthrall is to hold captive, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: to free is to release
final letter only
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A fragrant flower gives off a smell that captivates someone.
explanation.walkthrough: FREES and A together hold the I, so it slips in just before the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Freesias are South African flowering plants prized for their sweet fragrance, so one is an example of a fragrant flower.

clue.text: Transport by vehicle back to Cardiff right number

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: final letter only
R is the standard abbreviation for right
eight is a number

explanation.surface: Someone is driving back to the Welsh capital with the correct house number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back to Cardiff' reads as a journey home, but it means the final letter of Cardiff.
explanation.definitionFit: To freight goods is to carry them as cargo, by lorry, ship or train, which is moving them commercially by vehicle.

clue.text: Heavy criminal uses to repress S American city

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted out of order
to repress is to hold down and keep in, so one piece is shut inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
Rio de Janeiro in Brazil

explanation.surface: A violent thug uses force to subdue a South American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy' looks like a noun, a thug, but it is the definition as an adjective; 'criminal' then works as the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy and serious both describe something weighty, grave or lacking in lightness, as in a heavy or serious discussion.

clue.text: Pay back Pat, upset visiting French city base

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, and in a down-or-across reading that turns the letters backwards
a visitor goes inside someone else's place, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: to pat or rub is to stroke gently
Reims is the champagne capital in north-east France
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A person named Pat is upset about visiting a French city's military base.
explanation.walkthrough: Pat looks like a name, but it is the verb. Crosswords use base for E, the mathematical constant that is the base of natural logarithms.
explanation.definitionFit: To reimburse is to repay money that someone has spent or lost, so it means returning funds owed.

clue.text: Lead in grey I put on my dog

indicators.note: the lead is the front position, so only the opening letter is kept
putting one thing on another places them together, here after the exclamation

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
opening letter only
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone clips a grey leash onto their pet dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a dog lead but means first letter; 'my' is the exclamation, which Britons render as 'cor!'
explanation.definitionFit: The corgi is a short-legged Welsh herding breed, famously kept by Queen Elizabeth II, so it is a kind of dog.

clue.text: Hear some unsuspected trick in question?

blocks.note: first meaning: to make out what someone says
second meaning: a hidden snag that makes a question harder than it looks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear some' reads as a request to listen; the clue then splits into a verb meaning and a noun meaning of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: You can say 'I didn't catch that' for not hearing, and a trick question contains a hidden snag that wrong-foots the person answering.

clue.text: Lots mostly theologian claims that's idly scribbled down

indicators.note: mostly means not entirely, so the last letter is dropped
to claim something is to take hold of it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: DD is a Doctor of Divinity
OODLES means lots, losing its final letter

explanation.surface: A theologian makes many claims that someone has jotted down absent-mindedly.
explanation.walkthrough: DD, a Doctor of Divinity, stands for a theologian in crosswords; it splits to hold the shortened word for lots.
explanation.definitionFit: To doodle is to draw or write aimlessly while your attention is elsewhere, so a doodled thing was idly scrawled.

clue.text: Owner's command as dog went berserk?

indicators.note: going berserk means running wild, so the letters break out of their order

blocks.note: both words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: What a pet owner shouts when their dog runs wild and jumps up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue paints the scene: the shuffled words describe exactly when an owner would give this order.
explanation.definitionFit: Owners tell a dog that is jumping up at people or furniture to get down, an order to return to the floor.

clue.text: Check adequacy of lights for international games

blocks.note: to test is to check whether something is good enough
matches are lights, things you strike to light a fire

explanation.surface: Floodlights are being inspected ahead of international sporting fixtures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lights' suggests floodlights, but it means matches, the things you strike. Test matches are full international games of cricket or rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket and rugby a Test is a full match between national sides, so Test matches are international fixtures.
